source_text: Γυνή τις συνεβίου ἀνδρὶ ἀκολασταίνοντι, ἀκολασταίνουσα καὶ αὐτὴ πρότερον. Ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγματα ἔγνω, αὐτὴ ἐσωφρονίσθη καὶ τὸν ἄνδρα ὁμοίως σωφρονεῖν πείθειν ἐπειρᾶτο, τὰ διδάγματα ἀναφέρουσα, τήν τε μέλλουσαν τοῖς οὐ σωφρόνως καὶ μετὰ λόγου ὀρθοῦ βιοῦσιν ἔσεσθαι ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ κόλασιν ἀπαγγέλλουσα. Ὁ δὲ ταῖς αὐταῖς ἀσελγείαις ἐπιμένων ἀλλοτρίαν διὰ τῶν πράξεων ἐποιεῖτο τὴν γαμετήν. Ἀσεβὲς γὰρ ἡγουμένη τὸ λοιπὸν ἡ γυνὴ συγκατακλίνεσθαι ἀνδρί, παρὰ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον καὶ παρὰ τὸ δίκαιον πόρους ἡδονῆς ἐκ παντὸς πειρωμένῳ ποιεῖσθαι, τῆς συζυγίας χωρισθῆναι ἐβουλήθη. Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων, ὡς εῖς ἐλπίδα μεταβολῆς ἥξοντός ποτε τοῦ ἀνδρός, βιαζομένη ἑαυτὴν ἐπέμενεν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ ταύτης ἀνὴρ εἰς τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν πορευθεὶς χαλεπώτερα πράττειν ἀπηγγέλθη, ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδικημάτων καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται μένουσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁμοδίαιτος καὶ ὁμόκοιτος γινομένη, τὸ λεγόμενον παρ᾿ ὑμῖν ῥεπούδιον δοῦσα ἐχωρίσθη. Ὁ δὲ καλὸς κἀγαθὸς ταύτης ἀνήρ, δέον αὐτὸν χαίρειν, ὅτι, ἃ πάλαι μετὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν καὶ τῶν μισθοφόρων εὐχερῶς ἔπραττε, μέθαις χαίρουσα καὶ κακίᾳ πάσῃ, τούτων μὲν τῶν πράξεων πέπαυτο καὶ αὐτὸν τὰ αὐτὰ παύσασθαι πράττοντα ἐβούλετο, μὴ βουλομένου ἀπαλλαγείσης κατηγορίαν πεποίηται, λέγων αὐτὴν Χριστιανὴν εἶναι. Καὶ ἡ μὲν βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε, πρότερον συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῇ διοικήσασθαι τὰ ἑαυτῆς ἀξιοῦσα, ἔπειτα ἀπολογήσασθαι περὶ τοῦ κατηγορήματος μετὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῆς διοίκησιν, καὶ συνεχώρησας τοῦτο. Ὁ δὲ ταύτης ποτὲ ἀνήρ, πρὸς ἐκείνην μὲν μὴ δυνάμενος τανῦν ἔτι λέγειν, πρὸς Πτολεμαῖόν τινα, ὃν Οὔρβικος ἐκαλέσατο, διδάσκαλον ἐκείνης τῶν Χριστιανῶν μαθημάτων γενόμενον ἐτράπετο διὰ τοῦδε τοῦ τρόπου. Ἑκατόνταρχον εἰς δεσμὰ ἐμβαλόντα τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φίλον αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντα, ἔπεισε λαβέσθαι τοῦ Πτολεμαίου καὶ ἀνερωτῆσαι, εἰ, αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον, Χριστιανός ἐστι. Καὶ τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φιλαλήθη ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπατηλὸν οὐδὲ ψευδολόγον τὴν γνώμην ὄντα, ὁμολογήσαντα ἑαυτὸν εἶναι Χριστιανόν, ἐν δεσμοῖς γενέσθαι ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος πεποίηκε, καὶ ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ ἐκολάσατο. Τελευταῖον δέ, ὅτε ἐπὶ Οὔρβικον ἤχθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁμοίως αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον ἐξητάσθη, εἰ εἴη Χριστιανός. Καὶ πάλιν, τὰ καλὰ ἑαυτῷ συνεπιστάμενος διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδαχήν, τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν. Ὁ γὰρ ἀρνούμενος ὁτιοῦν ἢ κατεγνωκὼς τοῦ πράγματος ἔξαρνος γίνεται, ἢ ἑαυτὸν ἀνάξιον ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀλλότριον τοῦ πράγματος τὴν ὁμολογίαν φεύγει· ὦν οὐδὲν πρόσεστι τῷ ἀληθινῷ Χριστιανῷ. Καὶ τοῦ Οὐρβίκου κελεύσαντος αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι, Λούκιός τις, καὶ αὐτὸς ὢν Χριστιανός, ὁρῶν τὴν ἀλόγως οὕτω γενομένην κρίσιν, πρὸς τὸν Οὔρβικον ἔφη· Τίς ἡ αἰτία, τοῦ μήτε μοιχὸν μήτε πόρνον μήτε ἀνδροφόνον μήτε λωποδύτην μήτε ἅρπαγα μήτε ἁπλῶς ἀδίκημά τι πράξαντα ἐλεγχόμενον, ὀνόματος δὲ Χριστιανοῦ προσωνυμίαν ὁμολογοῦντα τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον ἐκολάσω; Οὐ πρέποντα Εὐσεβεῖ αὐτοκράτορι οὐδὲ φιλοσόφῳ Καίσαρος παιδὶ οὐδὲ τῇ ἱερᾷ συγκλήτῳ κρίνεις, ὦ Οὔρβικε. Καὶ ὃς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἀποκρινάμενος καὶ πρὸς τὸν Λούκιον ἔφη· Δοκεῖς μοι καὶ σὺ εἶναι τοιοῦτος. Καὶ τοῦ Λουκίου φήσαντος· Μάλιστα, πάλιν καὶ αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι ἐκέλευσεν. Ὁ δὲ καὶ χάριν εἰδέναι ὡμολόγει, πονηρῶν δεσποτῶν τῶν τοιούτων ἀπηλλάχθαι γινώσκων καὶ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα τῶν οὐρανῶν πορεύεσθαι. Καὶ ἄλλος δὲ τρίτος ἐπελθὼν κολασθῆναι προσετιμήθη.
thought_title: The case of the Christian woman, Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third Christian under Urbicus
orientation: Justin is reporting to the Roman Senate and people the events that happened under the urban prefect Urbicus, beginning with a Christian woman who separated from her unchaste husband.
pass_a_gloss: A certain woman lived with a husband who was acting licentiously, she herself also acting licentiously formerly. But when she learned the teachings of Christ, she herself was made chaste, and she was trying to persuade her husband likewise to be chaste, reporting the teachings, and announcing the punishment that is going to be in eternal fire for those who do not live chastely and with right reason. But he, remaining in the same licentious acts, was making his wife alienated through his deeds. For the woman, considering it impious for the rest to lie with a husband who was trying by every means to make paths of pleasure contrary to the law of nature and contrary to justice, wished to be separated from the marriage. And when she was entreated by her own people, who were advising her to remain still, since the husband would come at some time to hope of change, she remained, forcing herself. But when her husband, having gone to Alexandria, was reported to be doing more grievous things, so that she might not become a sharer in his injustices and impieties by remaining in the marriage and becoming a table-sharer and bed-sharer, she gave what is called among you a bill of divorce and was separated. But her noble and good husband, when he ought to have rejoiced that she had ceased from those deeds which she formerly did readily with servants and hired men, rejoicing in drunkenness and every vice, and that she wished him also to cease doing the same things, when she departed against his will, he made an accusation, saying that she was a Christian. And she submitted a little petition to you the emperor, asking first that it be permitted to her to arrange her own affairs, then to make a defense concerning the accusation after the arrangement of her affairs, and you granted this. But her former husband, not being able to speak against her any longer now, turned against a certain Ptolemy, whom Urbicus had summoned, who had become her teacher of the Christian teachings, in this manner. He persuaded a centurion, who had thrown Ptolemy into bonds and was a friend to him, to seize Ptolemy and to ask him if, this very thing only, he is a Christian. And Ptolemy, being a lover of truth and not a deceitful or false-speaking person in his mind, confessed himself to be a Christian, and the centurion made him to be in bonds, and for a long time he punished him in the prison. Finally, when the man was brought before Urbicus, likewise this very thing only was examined, whether he was a Christian. And again, knowing the good things in himself through the teaching from Christ, he confessed the school of divine virtue. For the one who denies anything either has condemned the matter and becomes a denier, or knowing himself unworthy and alien to the matter he flees the confession; none of which belongs to the true Christian. And when Urbicus commanded him to be led away, a certain Lucius, himself also being a Christian, seeing the judgment that had happened so irrationally, said to Urbicus: What is the cause, that you punished this man, who has been convicted of committing neither adultery nor fornication nor murder nor theft nor robbery nor simply any injustice, but who confesses the name of Christian as his appellation? You judge things not fitting for a pious emperor nor for a philosopher son of Caesar nor for the sacred senate, O Urbicus. And he, answering nothing else, also said to Lucius: You seem to me also to be such a one. And when Lucius said: Most certainly, again he commanded him also to be led away. And he confessed that he knew gratitude, knowing that he had been freed from such wicked masters and was going to the Father and King of the heavens. And another third one, coming forward, was also sentenced to be punished.

pass_b_english: A certain woman had lived with a husband who acted licentiously, and she herself had also acted licentiously before. But when she learned the teachings of Christ, she was made chaste, and she tried to persuade her husband likewise to be chaste, presenting the teachings to him and announcing the punishment that will come in eternal fire for those who do not live chastely and with right reason. He, however, continued in the same licentious acts and by his actions made his wife a stranger to him. For the woman now considered it impious to lie with a man who, contrary to the law of nature and contrary to justice, tried to make every path a path of pleasure, and she resolved to separate from the marriage.

When her own people entreated her to remain still, advising her in the hope that her husband would one day come to a change, she forced herself and remained. But when her husband went to Alexandria and was reported to be doing even worse things, she gave him what is called among you Romans a bill of divorce and separated, so that by remaining in the marriage and sharing his table and bed she might not become a partner in his injustices and impieties.

But this fine and noble husband of hers, when he ought to have rejoiced that she had stopped the acts she once did easily with servants and hired men, delighting in drunkenness and every vice, and that she wanted him also to stop doing the same things, when she departed against his will, he brought an accusation against her, saying that she was a Christian. And she submitted a petition to you, the emperor, asking first to be permitted to arrange her own affairs, and then to make her defense concerning the accusation after the arrangement of her affairs, and you granted this.

But her former husband, no longer able to speak against her at that time, turned against a certain Ptolemy, whom Urbicus had summoned, who had become her teacher in the Christian teachings, in this way. He persuaded a centurion, a friend of his, who had thrown Ptolemy into chains, to seize Ptolemy and ask him this one thing only: whether he was a Christian. And Ptolemy, being a man who loved truth and was not deceitful or false-speaking, confessed himself to be a Christian, and the centurion made him be put in chains and punished him in prison for a long time.

Finally, when the man was brought before Urbicus, he was examined in the same way on this one thing only: whether he was a Christian. And again, knowing the good things in himself through the teaching from Christ, he confessed that he was a Christian. For whoever denies anything either becomes a denier because he has condemned the matter, or because he knows himself unworthy and alien to the matter he flees confession; none of which belongs to the true Christian.

And when Urbicus ordered him to be led away, a certain Lucius, himself also being a Christian, seeing the judgment that had been made so irrationally, said to Urbicus: "What is the reason that you have punished this man, who has been convicted neither as an adulterer nor a fornicator nor a murderer nor a thief nor a robber nor simply as having done any wrong, but who confesses the name of Christian? Urbicus, you judge things not fitting for a pious emperor, nor for a philosopher son of Caesar, nor for the sacred senate."

And Urbicus, answering nothing else, also said to Lucius: "You seem to me to be such a one also." And when Lucius said: "Most certainly," Urbicus ordered him also to be led away. And Lucius confessed that he was grateful, knowing that he was delivered from such wicked masters and was going to the Father and King of the heavens. And another third man also came forward and was also sentenced to be punished.

edits.new: And Ptolemy, being a man who loved truth and was not deceitful or false-speaking

fixed: The petition to the emperor is correct: the source says βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε, 'she submitted a petition to you the emperor,' and the emperor granted it. The English accurately renders this; no change needed.

The phrase 'the teaching of divine virtue' renders τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς, which is a specific expression in the source, not merely 'Christian teaching.' The English is accurate; no change needed.

The source says φιλαλήθη ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀπατηλὸν οὐδὲ ψευδολόγον τὴν γνώμην ὄντα, 'being a lover of truth and not a deceitful or false-speaking mind.' The English 'mind' is a literal rendering of γνώμην, but it is awkward in English. I changed it to 'a man who loved truth and was not deceitful or false-speaking' to clarify that Ptolemy was a person, not a mind.
